options.why: Chose the concave down side; $f''(x) > 0$ is where the curve bends upwards, which is to the right of the inflection.
Used the $x$-value of the minimum turning point instead of the $x$-value of the point of inflection.
Gave the interval where the curve is decreasing, which is where $f'(x) < 0$, not where $f''(x) > 0$.

questions.solution_text:
The curve bends downwards to the left of the point of inflection and upwards to the right of it.
The inflection lies midway between the turning points at $x = 0$ and $x = 2$, so it is at $x = 1$.
$f''(x) > 0$ for $x > 1$

questions.question_text: Which correctly describes the stationary points of $y = 2x^3 + 3x^2 - 12x + 4$?

options.why: Swapped the natures; a cubic with a positive leading coefficient reaches its maximum at the left-hand stationary point.
Paired each $x$-value with the other point's $y$-value when substituting back into $y$.
Sign error factorising $6x^2 + 6x - 12$, reading the roots of $6(x + 2)(x - 1)$ as $x = 2$ and $x = -1$.

questions.question_text: Which statement about the stationary points of $y = 3x^4 - 8x^3 + 6$ is correct?

options.text: A horizontal point of inflection at $(0, 6)$ and a minimum at $(2, -10)$
A maximum at $(0, 6)$ and a minimum at $(2, -10)$
options.why: Assumed every stationary point is a turning point; at $x = 0$ the gradient is negative on both sides, so there is no turning.

options.text: A horizontal point of inflection at $(0, 6)$ and a maximum at $(2, -10)$
options.why: Sign error in $y''(2) = 144 - 96 = 48$, which is positive, so $x = 2$ is a minimum.

options.text: A minimum at $(0, 6)$ and a horizontal point of inflection at $(2, -10)$
options.why: Swapped the two stationary points; $y''$ is zero at $x = 0$, not at $x = 2$.

questions.question_text: Which gives the equations of both asymptotes of $y = \dfrac{2x - 1}{x + 3}$?

options.why: Sign error solving $x + 3 = 0$, reading the vertical asymptote off the constant rather than its solution.
Inverted the ratio of the leading coefficients; the horizontal asymptote is $\dfrac{2}{1}$, not $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
Made both errors: the sign of the vertical asymptote and the inverted leading-coefficient ratio.

questions.question_text: For $f(x) = xe^{-x}$ it is given that $f'(x) = (1 - x)e^{-x}$ and $f''(x) = (x - 2)e^{-x}$. Which gives the stationary point and the point of inflection?

options.why: Sign error in $f''(1) = -e^{-1}$, which is negative, so the stationary point is a maximum.
Swapped the roles of the two derivatives: $f' = 0$ gives the stationary point and $f'' = 0$ gives the inflection.
Sign slip solving $(1 - x)e^{-x} = 0$ and $(x - 2)e^{-x} = 0$, giving $x = -1$ and $x = -2$.
At $A$ the curve is rising and bending downwards, so $f'(x) > 0$ and $f''(x) < 0$ — both signs are wrong.
The curve is falling at $B$, but it is still concave down there, so $f''(x) < 0$.
The curve is concave up at $D$, but it is rising again past the minimum, so $f'(x) > 0$.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) < 0$ means the curve is falling, which happens between the maximum and the minimum.
$f''(x) > 0$ means the curve is concave up, which happens to the right of the point of inflection.
Only $C$ lies in both regions.
The answer is $C$.

questions.question_text: The curve $y = x^3 + bx^2 + cx + 7$ has a point of inflection at $x = 1$ and a stationary point at $x = 3$. What are the values of $b$ and $c$?

options.why: Sign error solving $27 - 18 + c = 0$; moving $9$ across gives $c = -9$, not $c = 9$.
Sign error solving $6 + 2b = 0$; dividing gives $b = -3$, not $b = 3$.
Made both sign errors, in solving $6 + 2b = 0$ and in solving $27 + 2bx + c = 0$ at $x = 3$.

questions.question_text: The curve $y = 2\cos x + x$ is defined for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$. Where are its stationary points?

options.why: Natures swapped; $y'' = -2\cos x$ is negative at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, giving a maximum there.
Solved $\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ instead of $\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ when setting $y' = 0$.
Used the turning points of $\cos x$ itself, ignoring the $+x$ term that shifts where the gradient is zero.

questions.question_text: The curve $y = x\ln x$ has one stationary point in its natural domain $x > 0$. What are its coordinates?

options.why: Sign slip evaluating $y$: $\ln\left(e^{-1}\right) = -1$, so the $y$-value is negative.
Solved $\ln x = 0$ instead of $\ln x + 1 = 0$, forgetting the second term of the product rule.
Solved $\ln x = 1$ instead of $\ln x = -1$, taking the reciprocal of the correct $x$-value.

questions.question_text:
The table gives the signs of $f'(x)$ and $f''(x)$ for a curve $y = f(x)$.

$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & x<2 & 2 & 2<x<5 & 5 & x>5 \\ \hline f'(x) & - & 0 & + & + & + \\ f''(x) & + & + & + & 0 & - \end{array}$

Which statement about the curve is correct?

options.text: A minimum at $x = 2$ and a point of inflection at $x = 5$
A maximum at $x = 2$ and a point of inflection at $x = 5$
options.why: Read the concavity backwards; $f''(2) > 0$ means concave up, so the stationary point is a minimum.

options.text: A minimum at $x = 2$ and a horizontal point of inflection at $x = 5$
options.why: Assumed $f'(x) = 0$ at every point of inflection; the table shows $f'(5) > 0$, so the tangent there is not horizontal.

options.text: A point of inflection at $x = 2$ and a minimum at $x = 5$
options.why: Swapped the two derivatives: $f'(x) = 0$ locates a stationary point and a sign change in $f''(x)$ locates an inflection.
